Name: Annotate, then the model reads the room
Definition: A session move in which participants work by hand on paper (annotating, sorting, writing), the LL captures the paper as images, and a model reads all of it at once to report patterns back to the room during the session.
Description:
From the LL's overview (undated) [1]:

- **COMPLIT 207, fall 2024:** "a full-class studio session where students annotated 3-foot-long physical printouts of the syllabus ... We captured the annotated syllabi and used the OpenAI Vision API to generate class-wide reflections in real time, prompting deeper discussion."
- **AI Tools for Language Instructors, fall 2024:** faculty hand-annotated "printed translations of the Harvard Mission Statement"; "Our team digitized the annotations and used AI to identify themes across participant responses. The workshop showed how AI can process large amounts of analog student work while preserving the pedagogical value of handwriting, translation nuance, and voice."

This term: the TF AI-comfort card sort, "12 table photos → CSV → chart" [2]. The Greatest Hits report (a synthesis) adds "Interactive Polling with Gen AI (live polls → AI finds patterns → discussion questions)" [3].
HowTo: From the record: print large (a 3-foot syllabus [1]); collect or photograph the paper (tables shot from above [2]); give the images to a vision model with a request for themes or a table; show the result on the studio screen and discuss [1][2].
WhyTo:
From the record: "AI can process large amounts of analog student work while preserving the pedagogical value of handwriting, translation nuance, and voice" [1]; the reflections were for "prompting deeper discussion" [1].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:** the caution the entry should carry.

1. Students see the raw photos beside the model's summary, so they can check what it missed.
2. Students' handwriting goes to a model only with their knowledge, said at the start.
HomeGameClassroom: Phone photos of each group's sheet, uploaded by the instructor to any chat model that reads images, with the summary projected. (Our suggestion.)
HomeGameDigital: A shared document or form instead of paper; the model reads the export. (Our suggestion.)

Name: The game show from the booth
Definition: A session run as a mock game show: the speaker or contestant performs on the studio floor while an operator in the control booth fires the show's cues (countdown, buzzer, music, title cards) onto the studio screen.
Description: Marlon, Nov 16, 13:23 (typed): Terry Gipson's EXPOS 40 session on public speaking is "ostensibly one of our most difficult-to-replicate-outside-of-the-studio activities ... In the session students engage in a mock game show activity, so we are creating a 'Home Game' version of it for him" [1]. The show is *Are You Serious?!*: a speaker has to stay serious while a buzzer and a countdown try to crack them [3]. The app (`ll-26-27/expos40`, built Nov 9) is "A keyboard sound board and a 1920×1080 stage for one operator to run Terry's game show 'Are You Serious?!' from the booth": key 1 the countdown, 2 the intro and hovering title, B the "Smile buzzer" [2]. The sessions this term were canceled; the home game is this week's build [3].
HowTo: From the app's README: run the board and the stage; the switcher takes the stage window full frame; the operator plays cues from the keyboard [2]. The rules are "written down nowhere the LL has found" [3].
WhyTo:
From the record: public speaking under playful pressure, in Terry Gipson's course [1][3].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:** what the game-show frame does for teaching beyond EXPOS 40.

1. Pressure without consequences: rehearsal for talks and oral exams. Marlon on play, Nov 16, about 17:17 (voice agent's record): "If people don't take the game seriously, it doesn't even work. People have to pretend to be invested, but you also don't want real harm to happen" [1].
2. A role for every student: contestant, host, operator, audience.
HomeGameClassroom: The home game: the board on a classroom laptop and projector, run by the instructor or a student; the accessibility research asks that "every action on a key, a visual for every meaningful sound, a timer the host can change or turn off" [3][4].
HomeGameDigital: The same board screen-shared in a call. (Our suggestion.)

Name: Cards
Definition: A set of printed cards, each holding one thing (a term, an idea, a role, a record, a challenge), which people draw, sort, deal, rank, lay out and link on a table, so that a body of material can be handled one piece at a time and rearranged.
Description:
Marlon, Nov 17, 07:13 (voice agent's record), in his list of LL mechanics: "Just cards" [1]. A card is small enough to hold one idea and to move by hand, so a group can sort, sequence, group or deal a whole body of material on a table and see the arrangement at once. The same deck can be read, played or photographed.

Sessions where the LL used them, from the record:

- **SOC-STD 98to (William Stafford), Sept 28, 2026: "Database construction with index cards."** Marlon's account: "A way of thinking about the material of the course. Comes out of Manovich's text on databases versus narratives." Groups brainstormed databases of the course and went in different directions; some reached "a database of infrastructural elements, 'which is what we anticipated'", and the next session is to "do the database of infrastructure, because we're going to build a game based on it" [2]. That game is Monday's (Nov 23) Stafford workshop.
- **The TF AI-comfort card sort** (Beyond the Chatbox use case, cited Sept 24, 2026): "12 table photos → CSV → chart" [3].
- **ENGL 189VG, session 1, Oct 26, 2026.** The story station: "You'll design a short dialogue tree using colored cards" [4]; Marlon's plan for the stations: "story dev in cards and unity" [5]. How the session went is not yet recorded [5].
- **The mic taste test** (FRENCH 30 and 40, and others): students "use adjective cards to describe quality: 'warm,' 'crisp,' 'muddy,' 'clear'"; and in entrepreneurship sessions, "moving storyboards with colored cards" [6]. (Both from the Greatest Hits report, a model's synthesis of the LL's HackMD record.)
- **TDM 98, Nov 5, 2026.** Forty challenge cards and a game-mechanics page; at Marlon's request a drawn card pops up full screen on black to be keyed over video ("we'll run that through atem as luma key"; built, not yet tested on the ATEM) [7].
- **Week 11, Nov 13 to 17, 2026.** The week's ideas and cards in `_content/ideas/` and `_content/cards/`, printed in cut-out sheets [11]. On Nov 16 Marlon proposed the physical card as the game object whose properties live digitally, read with a phone tap (see [The tap](tap-to-move.md)) [8].
HowTo:
1. **One thing per card.** Write or print one term, idea, role or record on each. Marlon's print spec for this week's cards: "a nice chunky 900 pt headline/title with a 500 weight descript in Inter", and for the size, "5.5" wide (a column of 11x17 vertically, with varying heights depending on how much text" [9].
2. **Print and cut.** "He prints on 11x17 (and Letter), cuts the cards, and uses them on tables and walls" [10]. This repo's reader prints cut-out sheets on Letter at `/ideas/print` (`?per=4|6|8`) and the cards at `/cards/print` [11].
3. **Give a move.** A deck is only a deck until the activity says what to do with it: draw three, rank, group, build a tree, deal one each. The ENGL 189VG station gives the move and a question ("Mapping out the dialogue, can you get the player to where you want them to go?") [4].
4. **Capture the arrangement.** Photograph the table from above when the arrangement is done; the card sort became data that way [3] (see [The overhead view](overhead-view.md)).

What goes wrong, from the record: too many cards to print ("There may be too many to print, but that's ok--we're learning", Marlon, Nov 15 [10]); printed cards drift from their fuller digital text, so the week chose "abbreviated print cards that match fuller digital text" and no QR codes [10]; color cards under a keyed camera key out if they are green (see [Green paper](green-paper-key.md)).
WhyTo:
From the record:

- **To think about the material as data.** Stafford, Sept 28: the index cards were "A way of thinking about the material of the course", leading to "how things change when you start designing something that's more spatial, more schema-ish" (Marlon) [2].
- **To turn a room's opinions into a chart.** The card sort's photos became a CSV and a chart [3].
- **To give students words for what they hear.** The adjective cards in the taste test [6].
- **To make a game object.** Marlon, Nov 16: the card is "the game object", its properties live digitally, and every player "can see different things about these cards" [8].
HomeGameClassroom: Index cards and markers, or a printed sheet cut into cards, need nothing a classroom lacks. The LL's print views make Letter sheets of four, six or eight cards [11]. A phone photo from above keeps the result [3].
HomeGameDigital:
**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. The deck on a shared board: this repo's `/ideas/board` and `/cards` views (whiteboard and node graph) [11], run by the instructor on the room's screen.
2. A shared online whiteboard where each student drags their own copy of the cards (any whiteboard app; none tested by the LL for this).
3. Physical cards with an NFC tag each, so a phone tap opens the card's digital side (the week's proof of concept; see [NFC tags](../technologies/nfc-tags.md)).

Name: The concept map, node graph or knowledge graph
Definition: A diagram of ideas as nodes joined by links (lines, arrows, labeled relations), made by hand with cards, paper and string or on a screen, so that a body of material, an argument or a system can be seen whole and rearranged.
Description:
Marlon, Nov 17, 07:13 (voice agent's record), in his list of LL mechanics: "concept map, or node graph, knowledge graph — those are all interesting", with "ways to achieve these physically, in regular classes, and then in digital ways" [1]. The three names cover a range: a concept map is drawn to show how ideas relate; a node graph is the same picture used to describe a process (each node does something, each link passes something on); a knowledge graph stores the nodes and typed links as data a program can query [8].

Where the LL has done it, from the record:

- **Visual argument-mapping.** The LL's overview: "help an Expository Writing course use visual argument-mapping as a way to understand core moves in academic writing" (undated) [2].
- **Conceptual diagrams of borders.** SOC-STD 98MR, spring 2025: students "used art supplies to create conceptual diagrams and speculative data visualizations" [2].
- **A database of the course in index cards.** SOC-STD 98to (William Stafford), Sept 28, 2026: "Database construction with index cards", where groups went from the course "qua course" to "a database of infrastructural elements" [3]. (A schema, the database's cousin of a concept map.)
- **The agent as a node graph.** Week 9 (ending Nov 6, 2026), Marlon on prompt chaining: "All of that can be understood as a node graph, or metaphorized as a system of human-like roles. 'The question is just which helps you get the best quality work done.'" [4]. He told the LLUFs that "each builds themselves a bot, or more than a bot: a node graph like that, with triggers and, if they wish, loops or heartbeats" [5].
- **The week's ideas as a graph.** Since Nov 13, 2026, this repo shows Marlon's idea cards as a node graph at `/ideas/graph` and the deck at `/cards` views, with saved arrangements [6]; Marlon on Nov 15: "I want to be able to view in multiple ways, as node graph, in manipulable form" [7].
- **A dialogue tree in colored cards.** ENGL 189VG, Oct 26, 2026: "You'll design a short dialogue tree using colored cards" [9], a node graph of a conversation.

A paper concept map as the whole activity of a named session was not found in what I read.
HowTo:
On a table, as we suggest from the sessions above (no record gives step-by-step instructions):

1. **One node per card or sticky note,** written large enough for the overhead camera or a photo.
2. **Lay out, then link.** Place the nodes on an 11×17 sheet or a whiteboard and draw the links in marker, labeling each with the relation ("causes", "is part of", "answers").
3. **Name the type of graph first.** A dialogue tree branches from one start [9]; an agent's node graph runs from a trigger [5]; a concept map has no start. Telling the group which they are making saves the first ten minutes.
4. **Capture it** from above (see [The overhead view](overhead-view.md)) or on the story board.

On a screen: this repo's `/ideas/graph` (built with `@xyflow/react`) moves nodes and saves arrangements to `_content/ideas/_layouts/` [6]; the week's research compares how Luhmann's slip box, Obsidian, Roam and Logseq, property graphs and RDF, and Tana store nodes and links [8].

What goes wrong, from the record: graphs grow past what a group can hold. Week 9: "We keep hitting this scale of ever more complex graphs: each agent is itself a complex loop-and-graph structure, and then there's the graph of all of those agents" [5].
WhyTo:
From the record:

- **To understand the core moves of academic writing** (the Expository Writing argument-mapping) [2].
- **To think about course material as a structure, not a sequence:** the Stafford index cards, after Manovich's "databases versus narratives" [3].
- **To choose between two ways of seeing a system:** "a node graph, or ... a system of human-like roles. The question is just which helps you get the best quality work done" (Marlon, week 9) [4].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:** what the concept map is for in this week's rooms.

1. TDM 155AI: map a game as a node graph of state and moves before building it.
2. Stafford: the database of infrastructure from Sept 28 drawn as a graph, which becomes the game's board.
3. Presenting: a speaker builds the map live under the overhead camera while talking, so the structure of the talk appears as it is told.
HomeGameClassroom: Index cards or sticky notes, a large sheet or the board, and a marker are enough; a phone photo keeps the result. (We suggest this; it is the common classroom form and needs nothing the LL has.)
HomeGameDigital:
**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. This repo's graph view, run by the instructor on the room's screen, with students' cards loaded from Markdown [6].
2. A note tool that draws links as a graph (Obsidian's links and Canvas are among the models in the week's research [8]); each student keeps their own vault.
3. A shared online whiteboard with connectors, for a group map made at once.

Name: The stage window and cue buttons
Definition: A live-event set-up in which one full-screen browser window on the projector is the stage, and every input (buttons, MIDI pads, trigger words, camera gestures) is a cue that changes what the stage shows or sounds.
Description: TDM 155AI, Nov 11, 2026: the class app's "spine is one contract: every mechanic fires a cue or sets a parameter on a full-screen `/stage` window for the projector", with buttons and "a QLab-style cue list, MIDI pads and dials ... trigger words and a script-following reader with surtitles, semantic cues, MediaPipe instruments and body zones"; the record says none of its mechanics is confirmed as used in class [1]. The run of show's plan: individual exercises (MIDI pad to cue, dial to parameter), then groups make "a short performance idea, a performer/reader, and cue operator" [2]. The EXPOS 40 app of Nov 9 has the same shape: a board window and a stage window that "talk over BroadcastChannel", so the switcher takes the stage as a full-frame source and "nothing is an overlay" [3].
HowTo: From the record: open the stage window full screen on the projector; run the cue board or launcher on another screen; map each input to a cue; rehearse with a manual backup ("A few cue words and a manual backup") [2].
WhyTo:
From the record: to let students make "a little performance" from several kinds of input, each learned separately "to isolate the different things students are learning to do" [1].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. Presenting: a speaker runs their own cues (images, sounds, titles) from a pad instead of a slide clicker.
2. Teaching performance: students script a short piece and assign a cue operator, learning timing and coordination.
HomeGameClassroom: A laptop on the projector, the stage in one window and the cue board in another; keys replace pads [2].

Name: Draw a box
Definition: A computer-vision trick for the overhead camera: a person draws a rectangle on paper in thick dark marker, software finds the largest four-sided shape and warps a video clip into it, so the drawing becomes a screen.
Description: Built for TDM 155AI, Nov 11, 2026 (Installations and Live Events): "pick the overhead camera (Mirror off), draw a rectangle in thick dark marker; OpenCV.js finds the biggest four-sided shape and the clip is warped into it", with voice or buttons to choose the clip [1]. The run of show made it optional: "Try draw-a-box only if the overhead station passed the morning test" [2]. The week's wrap-up lists "draw-a-box video under the overhead camera" among what the class app had, and says none of its mechanics is confirmed as used in class [3].
HowTo: From the record: the overhead camera, mirroring off; paper and dark markers under the room's light; test "overhead camera, dark rectangle, clip selection, stability under the room's light" in the morning [1][2]. Fallback if drawn boxes are unreliable: printed ArUco markers [1].
WhyTo:
**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. A first lesson in computer vision: what the camera "sees" in a drawing and when it fails.
2. Paper as a projection surface: students lay out a storyboard of boxes and fill each with a clip.
HomeGameClassroom: A laptop's webcam pointed down at paper runs the same page, if the page is shared or deployed. (Our suggestion; untested.)
HomeGameDigital: Not applicable: the mechanic is the paper.

Name: Green paper as a green screen
Definition: Chroma keying on a tabletop: a sheet of green paper lies under a camera, the switcher or software removes the green, and whatever sits on the paper (a drawing, a cut-out figure, a hand) appears over another picture, video or live feed.
Description:
The studio's green screen is a wall and floor a person stands on; green paper brings the same trick down to a table, where a group can work on it together under a camera. Marlon, Nov 17, 07:13 (voice agent's record), names "using green paper as a green screen... and the various things that makes possible" among the LL's mechanics, and at 07:26: "the green screen (and green paper) — chroma keying — is literally the way we connect and layer multiple video feeds" [1].

He had already described it on Aug 8, 2026, in a dictation for TDM 155AI (machine transcript, quoted as transcribed): "how our use of green screen to largely work with horizontally ... green paper is a misuse of the tool, but it creates all these opportunities for creativity and collaboration that are not typically the name of the game when you think of digital compositing" [2].

Keying in the LL's sessions, from the record:

- **HUM 2, Oct 21, 2025.** The prep checklist sets the switcher's keyers, "usual chromas on 1 and 2 / lumas on 3 and 4", loads "card stock ... for paper dolls", and during class puts "paper dolls on cam once they exist" [3].
- **The puppetry residency for TDM 129B** (April 8–10; the year is not in the note). The LLUFs were asked to stage and photograph "green screen layering" and "multi-plane camera rigs" for a visual guide [4]. The paper dolls are made from green screen footage: "Take footage of yourself on the green screen in the main studio", cut the still out in Photoshop, "Print - and be sure to print on thick!" [5].
- **On the full green screen stage:** AFVS 173F, spring 2025, students "embodied plant movements on a green-screen stage"; TDM 119B, spring 2025, a "full-body long shot on our green screen stage" with AI-generated backdrops; SLAVIC/TDM 121, spring 2024, poses on the green screen read by computer vision and fed to Stable Diffusion [6]. The Greatest Hits report (a model's synthesis of the HackMD record) adds "Luma key effects for creative compositing" in AFVS 173F [7].
- **The luma key relative.** Marlon's studio notes from 2022–23 list "invert paper + black marker for luma key over subject" among the studio's moves [8]; on Nov 5, 2026, he asked for TDM 98's challenge cards to pop up on "fullscreen black ... we'll run that through atem as luma key" (built; "Not yet tested on a real second display or the ATEM") [10].

Green paper under a camera in a named session: not found in the record I read. Marlon's Aug 8 dictation speaks of it as the LL's practice [2].
HowTo:
In the studio, from the record and the studio's routing:

1. **Camera.** An overhead camera above the table (see [The overhead view](overhead-view.md)), framed so the green paper fills the picture.
2. **Keyer.** Route the camera to a switcher input with a chroma key set; HUM 2's checklist keeps chroma keys on inputs 1 and 2 and luma keys on 3 and 4 [3]. In software, OBS's Chroma Key filter "Removes any instances of a given color from the Source ... Use this filter for green screens", with the key color green by default [11].
3. **Background.** Put the picture, video or second camera that should show through behind the keyed layer.
4. **Material.** Draw or cut out on non-green paper; lay it on the green. Card stock for figures that will be handled [3][5].

What goes wrong, from the record: anything green on the table disappears. The 2023 PSY 980T plan sets out the art supplies with "(avoid green paper )" [9], and by the same logic (ours, not the record's) green markers and green sleeves vanish too. We expect uneven light and shadows on the paper to make the key patchy, as with any key; the record's rule for top-down shots is even, soft light (see the overhead view's how-to). A luma key, the alternative, needs strictly black and white: TDM 98's stage cards mark which looks are "Luma-safe" [10].
WhyTo:
From the record:

- **Collaboration and play on a table, not a stage.** Marlon, Aug 8, 2026: green paper "creates all these opportunities for creativity and collaboration that are not typically the name of the game when you think of digital compositing" [2].
- **Connecting and layering feeds.** Marlon, Nov 17, 07:26 (voice agent's record): chroma keying "is literally the way we connect and layer multiple video feeds"; 07:26 also: "So green plays a role to connect, overlay, layer things" [1].
- **Puppetry and paper figures.** The residency guide was to show "TDM students ... which techniques to use for their own projects" [4].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:** what to say green paper is for in a teaching or presenting context.

1. Putting yourself in the source: students' cut-outs or hands placed over the film still, map or diagram they are analyzing, as a step toward a video essay.
2. A presenter's layer: a speaker draws on green paper and the drawing appears over their slides or over their own camera.
3. A shared table scene: several people move paper figures over one projected background, a puppet show made by the group.
HomeGameClassroom:
**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. Green paper, a phone on a stand pointed down, and a laptop running OBS with its Chroma Key filter [11], shown on the room's projector. (We suggest this; not tested by the LL.)
2. Skip keying: white paper and a thick black marker with a luma key or a "multiply" layer, which needs no green and keys a drawing cleanly (after Marlon's 2022–23 note [8]; not tested in a classroom).
HomeGameDigital:
- OBS (free, Windows, macOS and Linux) keys any camera with its Chroma Key filter [11]; its output can be shared to a call.
- Video-call apps have their own virtual-background green screen settings; we could not confirm a vendor page for Zoom's while writing this, so none is cited.

Name: The overhead view
Definition: A camera mounted above a table and pointed straight down, so that paper, objects and the hands working on them become a flat, readable picture: shown live on a screen for the room, sent to a call, or recorded.
Description:
The overhead view turns a tabletop into a frame. Whatever is laid on the table (a drawing, cut-up film stills, cards, a game board, a hand building something) is seen by everyone at once and can be recorded as it changes. Marlon, Nov 17, 07:13 (voice agent's record), asks of it "how it's valuable, which contexts you might want it in, and ways of achieving it outside the Learning Lab space" [1].

Sessions where the LL used it, from the record:

- **SCRB 111, Explainer Video Workshop, Sept 16, 2025.** Groups took a section of a research paper and "translated that section into a paper prototype + overhead camera for an explainer video segment" [3][4].
- **HUM 7, planned Oct 7, 2025.** Students do "brief formal analyses using cut-up film stills under an overhead camera, presenting a short mock video essay that rehearses the same analytical moves they'll use in their written papers" [5]. (A plan; the record I read does not say how it went.)
- **A workshop on nonverbal communication and visuals** (undated plan). The welcome is given at the overhead ("use overhead to visually facilitate welcome"), and in the visuals activity a few volunteers present "at the overhead" [6].
- **The three-station video essay workshop** (GENED 1145 and others), Station 1: "Students create visual arguments using overhead cameras" [7]. This comes from the Greatest Hits report, a model's synthesis of the LL's 2021–25 HackMD notes, not a first-hand record.
- **FYSEMR 68D, looms, Oct 1, 2026.** "students build looms, hammering in nails; overhead camera" [8]. The outcome is not recorded there.
- **TDM 155AI, Nov 11, 2026.** *Draw a box*: under the overhead camera, a student draws a rectangle in thick dark marker and the app plays a clip inside it; listed as optional, "only if the overhead station passed the morning test" [9][10].
- **Week 11, Nov 14 to 16, 2026.** Marlon proposed photographing the LL's board games from overhead before play and mid-game, to show what game state is [11]. On Nov 16 "Blue and Jordan set up four overhead cameras today" (17:07), and Marlon, in a typed post at 13:23, called four overhead cameras "an LL Mechanic" for "various multi-station gamified learning activities" [2] (see [Four overhead cameras](overhead-stations.md)).
- The LLUFs have also tested surfaces for it: "New Mechanic: chalk marker on dark paper under overhead" [12].
HowTo:
In the studio, from the record:

1. **Mount and frame.** The camera looks straight down at the table, the paper filling the frame with "slight border for context" [13]. Marlon's task for this week is "always-on positions that are predictable and reliable, with cameras mounted on the truss in both locations", plus "tabletop or truss-top cameras across the hall" [1].
2. **Light it evenly.** For top-down shots: "Even, soft lighting (overhead softbox or diffused natural light); minimize shadows" [13].
3. **Route it to the room.** The overhead is a camera input on the studio's switcher; the nonverbal workshop's plan sends the classroom TV's output to the overhead ("start with it on the OH, which i think is camera 2") and switches to a laptop later [6].
4. **Check the picture in the app you will use.** The Nov 11 class app asks you to "pick the overhead camera (Mirror off)" [10]; its run-of-show tests "overhead camera, dark rectangle, clip selection, stability under the room's light" in the morning [9].
5. **Record or grab stills.** For documentation stills from an overhead shot, the LL's stills workflow says: "have one with hands and one without hands" [14].

What goes wrong, from the record: shadows and uneven light [13]; a mirrored image when a browser treats the camera as a selfie camera [10]; computer vision that depends on the room's light [9]; and a tilted board, which puts reading pins "on the wrong spaces" (proposed fix: printed corner markers) [15]. Blurry hands are common enough that the stills workflow plans around them [14].
WhyTo:
From the record:

- **Ideas before software.** The Greatest Hits report (a synthesis, see above) says paper under the overhead "Removes 'I don't know the software' barrier" and makes iteration fast: "draw, photograph, adjust = 2 minutes" [7].
- **A rehearsal of the writing.** HUM 7's plan uses the overhead's mock video essay to rehearse "the same analytical moves they'll use in their written papers" [5].
- **Translating research for an audience.** SCRB 111 used it to turn a paper into an explainer segment [3].
- **Presenting.** The welcome and the volunteers' visuals at the overhead in the nonverbal workshop [6].
- **Many tables at once.** Marlon, Nov 16, 13:23 (typed): "one that we frequently use for various multi-station gamified learning activities" [2].
- **Seeing a game's state.** Marlon's Nov 14 plan for the board games [11].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:** which of these the entry leads with for this week's rooms.

1. Teaching: the overhead as the shared table, where a group's paper work becomes the room's text to discuss (SCRB 111, HUM 7).
2. Presenting: the overhead as the presenter's hands, drawing or arranging while speaking (the nonverbal workshop).
3. Games: the overhead as the referee's eye on the board, photographing state for a model to read (Nov 14 and TDM 155AI tomorrow).
HomeGameClassroom:
**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. A phone on a stand or arm above the desk, joined to a video call that the room's projector shows. (We suggest this; the LL's record has no session that did it.)
2. The room's own document camera, where the room has one. (We have not checked which Harvard rooms do.)
3. No live feed: photograph the table from above at set moments and project the photos, as in the photograph-the-state plan [11].
HomeGameDigital:
- **Apple's Desk View.** A Mac with an iPhone as its camera (Continuity Camera) can show the desk in front of it from above, beside your face (Apple's page title: "Use Desk View to show your face and desk on camera"). Desk View needs a "Mac using Continuity Camera with iPhone 11 or later, excluding iPhone 16e and iPhone SE models", or one of the newer Macs with a built-in camera that supports it; on macOS Sonoma or later it is opened "From the Video menu in the menu bar, choose Desk View", and it is shared through the video app's screen sharing [16]. Continuity Camera itself needs "macOS Ventura 13 or later" and "iOS 16 or later" [17]. Not tested by the LL.
- We suggest a second device in the call (a phone pointed down, muted) as the overhead feed in any video-call app; we have not confirmed a vendor page for this.

Name: Paper prototype under the camera
Definition: A first version of a video, a visual argument or an explainer made with paper (printed stills, cut-outs, drawings, text) and recorded or photographed under an overhead camera, before any editing software is opened.
Description: The Greatest Hits report (a model's synthesis of the LL's 2021–25 HackMD notes) calls paper prototyping "standard first step" from 2022–23 on, in the three-station video essay workshop and elsewhere, with a "Standard Workflow": sketch on paper, "Arrange printed images, text, and drawings on overhead camera", photograph iterations, pick the strongest, then "Transition to digital tools" [1]. On the record: SCRB 111, Sept 16, 2025, "a paper prototype + overhead camera for an explainer video segment" [2]; HUM 7, Oct 7, 2025 (plan), "cut-up film stills under an overhead camera" for "a short mock video essay" [3]; SLAVIC/TDM 121, spring 2024, "annotated printed frame-by-frame stills ... using arts supplies to make claims about ballet the way they might in something like a video essay" [4].

The report's reasons (a synthesis): it "Removes 'I don't know the software' barrier", gives "Rapid iteration (draw, photograph, adjust = 2 minutes)", and keeps the "Focus on ideas and composition, not technical execution" [1]. HUM 7's plan: it "rehearses the same analytical moves they'll use in their written papers" [3].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:** whether the entry presents paper first as a rule for every LL media workshop, or as one station among three.

1. A rule: paper before software, always.
2. A station: one of the three, alongside equipment and software.
HomeGameClassroom: Printed stills, scissors and a phone above the desk; the photos are the prototype. (Our suggestion, after the report's workflow [1].)
HomeGameDigital: Students arrange the stills in any slide or drawing app and export each version. (Our suggestion.)

Name: Photograph the state
Definition: Photographing a game from directly above before play and again after some turns, so the difference between the two pictures shows the game's state; the photo is then turned into a table or JSON, by a person or a vision model, and checked against the table.
Description:
Marlon, Nov 14, in a voice chat (as transcribed in the handoff back to Claude Code): "here's the game, and then take a photo of it"; the plan around it was overhead shots of the LL's board games (Monopoly, Risk, Life), "an initial neutral state" and then a game in progress, and for card tables "let's just go with lipstick cams" [1]. For TDM 155AI on Nov 18 it is a 30-minute activity: two photos of the same board, Claude turns the second into a game-state table, students check it, list "What the photo can't see" (hands, deck order, whose turn, deals made out loud), and split template from instance [2]. On Nov 16 "Madeleine worked a bit on initial tests of computer vision that can read game boards, starting with chess" (voice agent's record) [4].

An earlier relative ran this term: the TF AI-comfort card sort, "12 table photos → CSV → chart" [6].
HowTo:
From the activity and the week's research:

1. **Shoot from directly above,** the whole board in frame, under even light; the overhead camera or a phone on a stand [2]. Top-down views avoid pieces hiding each other, though similar pieces are harder to tell apart from above [3].
2. **Shoot at set-up and again after ten minutes** [2].
3. **Ask the model for state per region** (property, square, card) as JSON, then check by hand "especially for stacks, money piles, overlapping cards, and anything face-down" [3].
4. **Add anchors if needed:** printed markers at the board's corners give the camera the board's plane [5]; the research lists "visual anchors drawn on the image" and fiducial tags as fixes [3].

What goes wrong, from the research: on real photos from varied angles, a classic chess pipeline found the board in about a third of images; models read sparse grids well and dense boards badly (Claude 3.5 Sonnet at 0.985 cell accuracy on tic-tac-toe, 0.554 on chess, in a 2025 study); counts and positions are approximate; models hallucinate with confidence [3]. A tilted board puts pins "on the wrong spaces" [5].
WhyTo:
From the record: to show students that "a game is data plus the verbs that change it, and a player sees only a view of it", and that what a photo cannot see is the hidden information (the class activity's account, a proposal written for Marlon) [2]; Marlon's aim, Nov 14: "go from a board game to how you would represent the data of that board game as a game state" [2].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:** its use outside games.

1. Any table of hand work (a card sort, a concept map) photographed and turned into data, as the card sort was [6].
2. A test of the model: the class measures how often it reads the table right, a lesson in checking AI output.
HomeGameClassroom: A phone photo from above and any chat model that takes images; a hand-drawn grid on the board helps (after the research's anchors [3]).
HomeGameDigital: Screenshots of a digital board do the same; or the game exports its state directly (the activity's *Universal Paperclips* save file [2]).

Name: The place-setting map
Definition: A single large sheet, 11×17 inches, set in front of each person or pair like a place setting at a table: a printed or hand-drawn map of the task, which is the surface they write on, lay cards and pieces onto, and take away.
Description:
Marlon, Nov 17, 07:13 to 07:14 (voice agent's record): "Just cards. 11×17 paper is the technology, and the mechanic could be sort of the map, the table... the place setting... kind of place-setting-size map, essentially", to be achieved "physically, in regular classes, and then in digital ways" [1]. The sheet gives each seat its own territory on a shared table: big enough to hold a layout of cards, a diagram, a board, small enough to be one person's.

What the record shows nearby (a per-seat 11×17 map in a named session was not found in what I read):

- **The agenda on 11×17.** A workshop on nonverbal communication and visuals (undated plan): "use an 11 x 17 to write out the agenda for the workshop, modeling that tip" [2].
- **11×17 as the LL's print size.** Marlon's card print spec, Nov 15, 2026: "5.5" wide (a column of 11x17 vertically" [3]; "He prints on 11x17 (and Letter), cuts the cards, and uses them on tables and walls" [4]; the studio's Ricoh takes 11×17 in Tray 3 [5]; The Notebook's printing skill prints "by default 11x17" [6].
- **Maps on the table for a games session.** ENGL 189VG, Oct 26, 2026, prep: "large rolls of paper / game boards / video game maps printed (a couple large?)" [7].
- **Annotating a map.** SOC-STD 98MR, spring 2025: "students annotated satellite images of Harvard Yard and Cambridge, mapping binaries like 'home/exclusion' or 'open/surveilled' onto familiar terrain"; NEC 101, spring 2025, at wall scale (see [Map on the projected wall](projected-wall-map.md)) [8].
- **In games.** The week's research on strategy games notes *The Quiet Year* (Avery Alder, 2013), where "players draw a shared community map" [9].
HowTo:
1. **Decide what the sheet is a map of.** A board for a game, a template (a timeline, a grid, a dialogue tree's slots), a printed image to annotate, or a blank sheet with a frame.
2. **Print one per seat** on 11×17 (the studio's Ricoh, Tray 3 [5]; The Notebook's `mk-printing` skill for Markdown [6]). Portrait or landscape to suit the map.
3. **Set the table.** Sheet, cards, markers; leave room around it for the cards that are not yet placed.
4. **Capture it.** Each sheet fits the overhead camera's frame, so the arrangement can be shown to the room or photographed (see [The overhead view](overhead-view.md)).

What goes wrong: we have no record of it run this way yet. We expect cards to overhang a sheet when the deck is large (Marlon's cards are 5.5 inches wide [3], half the sheet's short side), and green ink or paper to vanish under a keyed camera (see [Green paper](green-paper-key.md)).
WhyTo:
Marlon's words give the shape (a map, a table, a place setting [1]) but not yet the teaching purpose. The record has the general case for printing things for the room: "inventories of game mechanics that are printable and displayable throughout the space" (Marlon, Nov 13) [10].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. **Each person's own board.** In a game, the sheet is the player's mat (resources, hand, secret information), and the table between the sheets is the shared board: the Stafford game's per-player state on paper.
2. **A template that carries the method.** The sheet is a printed scaffold (a timeline, a database schema's columns, a dialogue tree), so the activity's structure is in front of every student without instructions on the screen.
3. **A take-away record.** What a student builds on the sheet goes home with them, or is photographed for the class archive, so the map is both workspace and handout.
HomeGameClassroom:
**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. The same sheet on Letter or A4 (half the area), printed on any office printer, with cards cut smaller.
2. A tabloid printer is not needed: two Letter sheets taped side by side make 11×17 (17 by 11 inches).
HomeGameDigital:
**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. A PDF of the map that students annotate on a tablet or laptop and submit.
2. A shared online board, one frame per student or pair, the digital place setting; the instructor's view shows all frames at once.

Name: The secret on your phone
Definition: Each player's phone works as a private screen: it shows information only that player may see (a hand of cards, a secret role, a team, starting coordinates), while what everyone knows is on the table or the shared screen.
Description:
Marlon, Nov 17, 06:01 (voice agent's record): "the dealing of a hand, or something that's metaphorically a hand — the starting coordinates of some kind of game, your identity in a playful guessing game, your teammates — a revealing of asymmetrical information. Clearly this could just be done with phones; people play those Jackbox-type games where they input codes and share that kind of information... but the idea of a card for each position around the table, people tapping their phones there and then seeing whatever the secret information is on their phone, is probably a good initial proof of concept" [1]. The day before: "Things involving asymmetrical information on the phone: good" [2]; and "Asymmetrical information, a key mechanic all week" [3].

Not yet run as a phone game; the proof of concept is for this week [1].
HowTo:
As proposed in the record: one tagged card per seat; each player taps the card at their seat and sees their secret [1]. Without tags: each player opens the game's link and joins with a code [1]. Phones on the same network as the laptop, or the game deployed [4].

What goes wrong: a player can show their phone to a neighbour, as with any hand of cards (our note); and a tag URL can be loaded without the card [4].
WhyTo:
From Marlon: "a revealing of asymmetrical information" [1].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:** what the private screen does in teaching.

1. Roles in a role-play or simulation (the Stafford game's players each holding a different brief).
2. A private answer before a public reveal, so no one anchors on the first voice.

Name: Station rotation
Definition: A session format: the room is divided into a few stations, each set up for one kind of work (often paper, equipment and software), and small groups move from station to station on a fixed clock until everyone has done each.
Description:
The Greatest Hits report (a model's synthesis of the LL's 2021–25 HackMD notes) calls the "three-station rotation format (15-20 minutes each)" the LL's most successful pattern, with three archetypes: "Conceptual/Low-Tech", "Equipment/Hands-On" and "Digital Tools" [1]. The LL's own overview describes multi-station and multi-zone workshops for AFVS 173F, SOC-STD 98MR, NEC 101 ("rotating teams") and language faculty, among others [8].

This term, from the record:

- **AI Open Studio re-run of TDM 155AI class 1, Sept 10:** "keep it at three: the table, the computers for the 'I Want' song, and the dark corner for the written self-portrait demo" [2].
- **TDM 155AI class 3, Sept 23:** "four stations (studio lights, cameras, camera obscura and projection, desk video kit)" [3].
- **Week 6 skills class, Oct 14:** "Video generation with AI / Block printing" among three stations [4].
- **ENGL 189VG session 1, Oct 26:** "Students rotate through three stations. Each station mixes the digital, the physical, and AI" [5].
- **TDM 155AI, Nov 11 (planned):** MediaPipe and button launching "kept apart in the rotation 'to isolate the different things students are learning to do'" [6].
- **Tomorrow, Nov 18:** Marlon, 05:12 (voice agent's record): the Stafford game "could be one of the stations" [7].
HowTo: From the Greatest Hits report's replication guide [1]: an introduction (5 minutes), three rounds of 20, a closing reflection; one staff member per station plus a coordinator; "station instruction cards (brief bullet points)" at each; documentation from the overhead camera afterwards.
WhyTo:
The Greatest Hits report's reasons (a synthesis): it "Divides class into manageable groups (5-8 students per station)", "Creates movement and energy in the room", "Allows for differentiated instruction", and students "experience full pipeline: concept → creation → refinement" [1]. Week 10's: to "isolate the different things students are learning to do" [6].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:** what to say about rotation vs. choice.

1. Fixed rotation: everyone does every station (the classic format).
2. Open stations: students choose and stay, as at an open house, with the host moving people on.
HomeGameClassroom: Tables as stations, a printed card at each, a timer on the projector; the instructor as the one roaming staff member. (Our suggestion.)
HomeGameDigital: Breakout rooms as stations, rotated on a clock, each with its instruction card pinned in the room's chat. (Our suggestion.)

Name: The story board
Definition: A large vertical board onto which the week's physical traces (images, drawings, notes, prints) are gathered as one story, which people then tell to a camera standing in front of it; the recordings go into an archive for storytelling.
Description:
Marlon, Nov 13, 2026 (dictated): "all term long, the Learning Lab undergrad fellows, or LLUFs, have worked with Jordan to collect all the materials, images, drawings, notes that people create in the Learning Lab studio over the course of the week, and then put those together onto one of the large four-by-eight vertical whiteboards that we have in the studio as a kind of story of the week. And then we stand in front of the board and record ourselves talking about it. And that's one of the core mechanics of storytelling" [1]. There are three boards, rotated; when one is retired, "between two and seven" of its stories go onto "a large gray wall next to the boards", some as "pasted constellations or little micro installations" [1].

From the term's record: week 3, Sept 25: "Every week we do a giant whiteboard installation. Name: The tap
Definition: A move made by touching a phone to a physical card with an NFC tag in it: the tap opens the card's digital side, which can show its current properties (a price, hit points, an owner) and record an action that changes the game's state.
Description:
Marlon, Nov 16, 17:31 (voice agent's record), "Core idea ... the physical card as the game object, its properties digital": "The card is the object"; its properties "live digitally, rather than hard-written onto the card"; they are "flexible and dynamic. You can rebalance the game as gameplay develops"; and "The tap is how you update state ... Tapping isn't just looking; it's the move that changes the game." His example is Monopoly: "you tap the property card to see how much it costs, and presumably buy it too." He adds: "I think there's a lot of promise" [1]. At 17:34: "every single thing you'd attach to a game object in Unity", including "decorative and aesthetic things, strategic values like prices, and of course history" [1].

What exists, from the record:

- Tags written and read with phones, Nov 16 evening; on iPhone a banner comes first [2] (see [NFC tags](../technologies/nfc-tags.md)).
- *Every tap is a row* (`/proto/hybrid/every-tap-is-a-row`, Nov 15): every tap, counted or not, is a row in a log, and the board is those rows replayed; it runs on keys, clicks or a USB reader [4].
- A tabletop build (one table, 8 to 12 cards, 2 to 4 phones) planned Nov 16, "Not launched" [5].
- For TDM 155AI on Wednesday, Nov 18, designing a game with the tags "will be one of the options for people" [2].
HowTo:
1. **One URL per card,** `http(s)://<host>/tap/<card-id>`, written to its tag [3].
2. **The page at that URL knows the player** (a join step or a code) and shows what this player may see of this card, with the actions the game allows [1][3].
3. **Every tap writes a row** (who, which card, when, what), so the game's state can be rebuilt from the log [4].
4. **Tap flat:** "lay cards flat and dip the top of the phone onto them"; stacked cards interfere [2].

What goes wrong: the iPhone's banner makes each tap two touches [2][3]; a URL can be copied and loaded without the card [3]; and Marlon's open question, "where it feels natural and pleasing, as opposed to clumsy and annoying" [1].
WhyTo:
Marlon's reasons (Nov 16, 17:31 to 17:34) are the ones above: a concrete object with flexible digital properties, rebalancing in play, and "Asymmetrical information, a key mechanic all week: every player can see different things about these cards by looking at them" [1].

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:** the tap's use outside a game.

1. Revealing a source: a card on the table stands for a document; the tap opens it, and the log shows which sources a group consulted.
2. Recording a choice: each tap is a vote or a commitment, so the class's decisions become data to discuss afterwards (the *Every tap is a row* idea [4]).
HomeGameClassroom:
Tags are cheap and students' phones are the readers [3]: send the cards and a deployed URL.

**Proposed, for Marlon to choose:**

1. NFC cards plus a QR code on each, for phones without NFC.
2. No tags: a short code printed on each card, typed into the game page.
HomeGameDigital: Clicking a card on screen is the tap; the log and the state change work the same [4].
